title: An evaluation model of college coaches

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical page 1 is the contest Summary; physical page 2 is the contents page; physical page 3 is printed page 2, and physical page 38 is printed page 37.

notes: All 38 local UTF-8 page text files were read in bounded physical-page ranges with truncation gaps explicitly reread.
All 38 rendered pages were visually reviewed through isolated JPEG proxies no larger than 288627 bytes.
No original full-page PNG, embedded base64 image, contact sheet, or multi-image tool result entered model transport.

section_map.summary: The title frames the deliverable as an evaluation model rather than an unqualified list of famous coaches.
The summary previews four indicators, fuzzy-consistent weights, grey ranking, cross-sport application, time correction, gender discussion, and two stability checks.
The task paragraph identifies the Sports Illustrated audience, the all-time cross-era ranking decision, and the required time and gender discussion.
The introduction moves from qualitative coach evaluation to a quantitative four-indicator workflow and names the two-stage model.
The overview separates factor-weight estimation from grey relational ranking and motivates the method by limited data availability.
The notation and definitions bind fuzzy matrices, indicator weights, reference arrays, grey coefficients, and evaluation outputs.
The weighting section converts a three-level preference matrix to a fuzzy-consistent matrix and derives a normalized root-method weight vector.
The ranking section forms an ideal coach from per-indicator maxima, normalizes data, computes grey coefficients, and aggregates a relational degree.
The application defines four indicators, filters Division I basketball coaches by wins, and traces the roster to Wikipedia and NCAA sources.
The calculation tables expose normalized basketball data, grey coefficients, ranks, and transfer of the same interface to football and ice hockey.
The external comparison places selected model lists beside media rankings as a plausibility check, not independent validation.
The time analysis groups careers by starting era, plots group means, applies one-way ANOVA, and introduces an inverse-average correction to winning percentage.
The gender section applies the same indicators and weights to a women-basketball roster and reports a top-five list.
The entropy check derives near-equal objective weights and compares its top-ten order with the fuzzy-consistent result.
A second stability check changes the pairwise importance order, recalculates ranks, and compares the resulting top ten.
The sensitivity section varies the grey distinguishing coefficient from 0.4 to 0.6 and claims the top-ten set is unchanged.
The closing assessment credits convenience and portability while acknowledging roster, award-count, and historical-correction limitations.
The references identify coach-evaluation, decision-weighting, and entropy sources but do not freeze the actual ranking dataset.
The appendix prints four sport rosters and MATLAB-style routines while retaining local paths, undefined inputs, and missing source spreadsheets.
The final article translates the four-indicator method and three top-five lists into an audience-facing narrative.

assumptions.summary: The ordinal priority championship > winning percentage > wins > coach awards can be represented with 0, 0.5, and 1 pairwise entries.
The best observed value of every benefit indicator forms a meaningful fictitious ideal coach.
Division I status and a sport-specific win threshold define an adequate candidate roster.
The same four indicators and weight semantics transfer across basketball, football, ice hockey, and gender.
Starting-career era is an adequate proxy for changes in competitive opportunity.
An inverse weighted-era average is a valid correction for winning percentage.
The women-basketball roster is sufficient to conclude that gender does not affect factor selection or weights.
Entropy-derived discrimination weights provide an informative alternate weighting check on the same roster.
Top-ten similarity after changing factor priority or rho is sufficient evidence of model stability.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The four benefit indicators are career wins, winning percentage, NCAA championships, and a sum of selected coach awards.
Basketball candidates are taken from a Wikipedia 600-win list, filtered to Division I, and linked to NCAA record sources.
The source prints the preference matrix, fuzzy-consistent matrix, and final weight vector.
Normalized basketball records use each column's observed range and a per-factor ideal of one.
Football and ice-hockey tables redefine championship and award columns before applying the shared ranking interface.
Basketball start years form five era groups; the source reports group means, plots, and two ANOVA tables.
Women-basketball records supply the same four fields for a separate top-five calculation.
Entropy weighting yields approximately equal weights 0.2493, 0.2492, 0.2508, and 0.2507.
Appendix pages 30-33 print candidate rosters and sport-specific award component columns.
Appendix pages 34-36 print MATLAB-style weighting, entropy, normalization, and grey-correlation fragments with local file paths.

results_trace.summary: The primary basketball top five are John Wooden, Adolph Rupp, Mike Krzyzewski, Dean Smith, and Jim Boeheim.
The reported football top five in Table 7.1 are Bear Bryant, Jim Tressel, Tom Osborne, Bobby Bowden, and Woody Hayes.
The reported ice-hockey top five are Jerry York, Vic Heyliger, Jack Parker, Ron Mason, and Ned Harkness.
The source reports a downward historical pattern in winning percentage while finding no stable time pattern in wins or championships.
After the post-1950 correction, Mike Krzyzewski leads the adjusted basketball list.
The women-basketball application ranks Pat Summitt first and claims no gender-dependent metric change.
Entropy weighting preserves the same basketball top-ten set with small order changes.
Changing factor priority produces small top-ten order changes in the reported table.
The source claims rho values 0.4, 0.5, and 0.6 leave the top-ten list unchanged.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The summary previews indicators, weighting, ranking, historical adjustment, and checks before detail, but award status alone does not prove why judges valued it.
The before/after table makes the intended historical correction visible, without validating its scale or fairness.
The article converts technical results into an audience-facing list, without proving external ranking truth.

weaknesses.summary: The audience is repeatedly called Sports Illustrator although the requested publication is Sports Illustrated.
The printed vector order follows wins, percentage, championships, awards, but the prose assigns 0.2169 to championships and 0.3527 to wins, conflicting with the matrix rows.
The grey comprehensive equation prints a score vector with n entries even though candidate count is m, and index use alternates between factor and candidate roles.
Eligibility thresholds differ by sport and exclude notable low-win coaches without a sensitivity analysis of the candidate boundary.
Coach Awards aggregate heterogeneous honors through a hand-selected list with no provenance snapshot, duplicate policy, or comparability rule.
The football model list in Table 9 conflicts with Table 7.1 and the final article; it substitutes Bowden, Warner, Stagg, and Paterno for the stated computed order.
External media lists use different candidate universes and methods, so overlap is not independent validation.
One-way ANOVA evaluates equality of group means, but the text interprets its p-values as differences of variances.
The inverse correction produces winning percentages above one, including 1.37, without redefining the metric or explaining downstream normalization.
After excluding two extreme coaches the paper treats p=0.08 as support for a correction, although failure to reject equal group means weakens that rationale.
The football p=0.07 argument similarly treats non-significance as justification for applying the moving-average correction.
The no-gender-effect conclusion comes from one women-basketball roster without a formal sex/gender comparison or cross-sport test.
The entropy prose reverses the usual relation between dispersion and entropy in places, and the extreme-value transformation is not clearly specified.
Table 21 assigns the main model's John Wooden, Adolph Rupp, Mike Krzyzewski, and Jim Boeheim scores to different names, contradicting Table 5.
The sensitivity conclusion checks a reported top-ten list but does not quantify score or rank uncertainty, roster instability, or simultaneous parameter changes.
Appendix basketball rows place career-start years under an award-component header for several coaches, indicating a table-schema or header alignment defect.
The entropy code computes an adjusted y matrix and then overwrites it with x divided by column sums plus one before entropy calculation.
The total-model code reads local spreadsheets, assumes an existing x in the entropy fragment, writes to a desktop path, and omits files, versions, and an executable wrapper.
No frozen source data, complete calculation package, uncertainty analysis, or independent held-out validation is supplied.
